title: System and User Security
summary: Accounts, groups, sudo and login history
markdown:
Read completely **chapter 15 and laboratory 15**. Below is a summary of all their educational content: theory, commands with descriptions and examples of output, analysis of user and group files, as well as self-test questions.

**Examples of output for training:** UID, GID, dates and users on another system may be different. Password hashes have been shortened. I did not run the commands from the laboratory.

There are several inaccuracies in the source material - they have been corrected and explained below.

---

**1. What you need to know for the exam**

The topic is indicated in the chapter **5.1 — Basic Security and Identifying User Types**, weight - **2**.

You need to be able to:

- differentiate between root, regular and system users;
- explain UID and GID;
- distinguish between main and supplementary groups;
- read entries `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/group`;
- understand password and account expiration dates;
- use `su` and `sudo`;
- find out information about users through `id` and `getent`;
- view current sessions via `who` and `w`;
- view login history via `last`.

Basic commands:

```text
su
sudo
exit
id
getent
head
tail
grep
ls -l
man
who
w
last
```

---

**2. User, account and rights**

**Account - user account** determines on whose behalf processes are running and what resources are available to them.

File permissions in the regular model Linux are considered for:

| Category | Meaning |
|---|---|
| User / owner | File owner |
| Group | File group |
| Others | Other users |

Groups allow you to grant access to multiple users at once.

For example:

```text
Users alice and bob are members of the group project.
The file belongs to the group project.
Group has read permission.
→ alice and bob can gain access through group membership.
```

**Group membership in itself does not mean full access:** you need to look at what rights are granted to the group for a specific file or directory.

---

**3. Three main types of users**

| Type | Purpose | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Root / superuser** | System administration | `root` |
| **Regular / standard user** | Normal human work | `sysadmin`, `alice` |
| **System / service account** | Running services and background tasks | `sshd`, `bind`, `syslog` |

**Root is defined primarily by UID `0`.**

```text
UID 0 → privileged account
```

Name usually `root`, but the key value for the system is the numeric identifier.

**UID — User ID**, user ID.

**GID — Group ID**, group identifier.

The system stores file owners as numeric identifiers. The programs display human-friendly names, matching them with UID and GID.

**Ranges UID from chapter:**

- in older systems, regular users often started with `500`;
- in many other systems - with `1000`;
- low UID are usually allocated to system accounts.

**Don’t memorize `1–499` as a universal range of system users.** Ranges vary by distribution and settings; for user creation tools they can be specified in `/etc/login.defs`. [Documentation `login.defs`](https://www.man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/login.defs.5.html)

---

**4. Why you shouldn’t always work as root**

Programs inherit the rights of the user under whose name they are launched.

If a browser, email client, or random command is run as root, the consequences of an error or compromise can affect the entire system.

Principle:

> For normal work, use a regular account. Get administrative rights for the necessary actions.

Root has extensive capabilities to bypass normal file permissions. At the same time, a phrase from the laboratory «root can read any file» should be understood as a simplification: there are additional access control mechanisms and technical limitations.

**Ubuntu:** by default the password root is usually locked and administrative actions are performed through `sudo`. The account root itself exists. In the training virtual machine, login through `su` is specifically permitted. [Documentation Ubuntu](https://ubuntu.com/server/docs/how-to/security/user-management/)

---

**5. `su`: launching another user’s shell**

General syntax:

```text
su [parameters] [user]
```

If the user is not specified, it is assumed **root**.

**Command `su` — open shell root without full login environment.**

```console
sysadmin@localhost:~$ su
Password:
root@localhost:/home/sysadmin#
```

The current directory is usually saved.

**Command `su -` — open login shell root.**

```console
sysadmin@localhost:~$ su -
Password:
root@localhost:~#
```

In a normal configuration, you are prompted **target user password**, here is root.

In the laboratory password root:

```text
netlab123
```

**Equivalent options from the chapter:**

```text
su -
su -l
su --login
su - root
```

They start the root shell in login mode.

**What does the login mode give:**

- go to target user’s home directory;
- preparing his environment;
- setting the appropriate variables, including `HOME`, `SHELL`, `USER`, `PATH`;
- launch shell as login shell.

This is described in [documentation `su`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/su.1.html).

**Command `su - bob` — go to user bob.**

```console
sysadmin@localhost:~$ su - bob
Password:
bob@localhost:~$
```

In a normal situation, the password is entered **bob**. For root, authentication rules may allow switching without the target user’s password.

**Important:** `su` is not only intended to go to root.

---

**6. `id` after switching and `exit` to return**

The shell prompt usually shows the user, but can be customized. To check use `id`.

**Command `id` — show the IDs of the current process and its group.**

After `su -`:

```console
root@localhost:~# id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

Here:

```text
uid=0 → execute the command as root
```

**Command `exit` — terminate the current shell.**

```console
root@localhost:~# exit
logout
sysadmin@localhost:~$
```

After this:

```console
sysadmin@localhost:~$ id
uid=1001(sysadmin) gid=1001(sysadmin) groups=1001(sysadmin),4(adm),27(sudo)
```

**`exit` after `su` returns to the previous shell.** If you run it in your original shell, you can end your terminal session.

Typically:

```text
$ → regular user prompt
# → prompt root
```

Symbols `$` and `#` from the examples does not need to be entered.

---

**7. `sudo`: command execution with different rights**

General syntax:

```text
sudo [parameters] command
```

By default, the target user is usually **root**.

**Command without necessary rights:**

```console
$ head /etc/shadow
head: cannot open '/etc/shadow' for reading: Permission denied
```

**Command `sudo head /etc/shadow` — read the beginning of the protected file as root.**

```console
$ sudo head /etc/shadow
[sudo] password for sysadmin:
root:$6$SALT$HASH:20000:0:99999:7:::
daemon:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
bin:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
sys:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
sync:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
games:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
man:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
lp:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
mail:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
news:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
```

`SALT` and `HASH` here are symbols.

**In normal configuration `sudo` prompts for the calling user’s password**, that is `sysadmin`, and not root.

Matching the passwords root and sysadmin in the lab does not change this rule.

**Right to use `sudo` must be configured.** Knowing your own password is not enough.

In the training Ubuntu permission is associated with the group `sudo`. Other systems may use different groups and rules.

**An additional example is to check on whose behalf the command is being executed:**

```console
$ sudo id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

Next command without `sudo` is executed again by a normal user:

```console
$ id
uid=1001(sysadmin) gid=1001(sysadmin) groups=1001(sysadmin),4(adm),27(sudo)
```

**`sudo` does not turn the original shell into root.**

---

**8. Timeout `sudo`: conflict in files**

The chapter states **5 minutes**, in the laboratory - **15 minutes for many Ubuntu**.

The correct general rule is:

> After successful authentication `sudo` may not prompt you for a password again for a while. The duration is determined by the settings.

This is the validity period of the stored authentication confirmation.

**It does not mean:**

- that all commands for the next 15 minutes are executed as root;
- that an already running administrative program will be forcibly stopped by a timeout.

The new administrative command still requires `sudo`.

The setting is called `timestamp_timeout`. The behavior and password prompt depends on the policy. [Documentation `sudoers`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/sudoers.5.html)

**Benefits `sudo` from the chapter:**

- explicit indication of administrative action;
- ability to allow certain commands;
- action logging;
- there is no need to share the password root with all administrators.

Log entries can contain user, command, date and time.

---

**9. Main difference `su` and `sudo`**

| Question | `su -` | `sudo command` |
|---|---|---|
| Main action | Opens another user’s shell | Runs the specified command |
| Default user | Root | Typically root |
| Whose password is usually needed? | Target user | Caller |
| What happens next? | Work continues in a new shell | After the command the normal prompt is returned |
| How to return? | `exit` | Usually a separate output is not needed |
| Is it possible to work as something other than root? | Yes, specify a user | Yes, with the policy enabled |
| Do you need to configure permissions? | Rules apply `su`/PAM | Policy in effect `sudo` |

**`sudo` also works on systems where the password root is enabled.** It is not limited to systems with the password locked root.

---

**10. Basic user and group files**

| File | What it contains | Normal access |
|---|---|---|
| `/etc/passwd` | General information about local users | Usually read by everyone |
| `/etc/shadow` | Password hashes and their expiration dates | Limited |
| `/etc/group` | Groups and Additional Memberships | Usually read by everyone |
| `/etc/gshadow` | Secure group information, including group passwords | Limited |

All four files are text record databases.

Main field separator:

```text
:
```

**Remember the number of fields:**

```text
/etc/passwd → 7
/etc/shadow → 9
/etc/group  → 4
```

---

**11. `/etc/passwd`: complete analysis of seven fields**

Example from files:

```text
sysadmin:x:1001:1001:System Administrator,,,,:/home/sysadmin:/bin/bash
```

General format:

```text
name:password:UID:GID:comment:home:shell
```

| № | Field | Example value | Explanation |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Name | `sysadmin` | Username |
| 2 | Password placeholder | `x` | Password information is in shadow |
| 3 | UID | `1001` | User ID |
| 4 | GID | `1001` | primary group |
| 5 | Comment / GECOS | `System Administrator,,,,` | Information field |
| 6 | Home directory | `/home/sysadmin` | Home directory |
| 7 | Shell | `/bin/bash` | Login shell |

**Field 2 — `x`:**

```text
x ≠ password
x ≠ no password
x → in use shadow- entry
```

**Field 5 - comment:** may contain your real name and other information. Commas don’t separate main fields `/etc/passwd`; the main separator is a colon.

**Field 6 - home directory:**

```text
/home/bob → typical directory bob
/root     → typical home directory root
```

**Field 7 - login program:** is not necessarily Bash. The system account here may have `/usr/sbin/nologin` or `/bin/false`.

Example root:

```text
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
```

Reading:

```text
Name: root
UID: 0
primary group: GID 0
Home directory: /root
Shell: /bin/bash
```

Format confirmed [documentation `passwd(5)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/passwd.5.html).

---

**12. View commands `/etc/passwd`**

**Command `head /etc/passwd` — show the first 10 lines.**

```console
$ head /etc/passwd
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/bin/sh
bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/bin/sh
sys:x:3:3:sys:/dev:/bin/sh
sync:x:4:65534:sync:/bin:/bin/sync
games:x:5:60:games:/usr/games:/bin/sh
man:x:6:12:man:/var/cache/man:/bin/sh
lp:x:7:7:lp:/var/spool/lpd:/bin/sh
mail:x:8:8:mail:/var/mail:/bin/sh
news:x:9:9:news:/var/spool/news:/bin/sh
```

**Command `tail -5 /etc/passwd` — show last five lines.**

```console
$ tail -5 /etc/passwd
syslog:x:101:103::/home/syslog:/bin/false
bind:x:102:105::/var/cache/bind:/bin/false
sshd:x:103:65534::/var/run/sshd:/usr/sbin/nologin
operator:x:1000:37::/root:/bin/sh
sysadmin:x:1001:1001:System Administrator,,,,:/home/sysadmin:/bin/bash
```

Double colon:

```text
::
```

means empty field between delimiters.

**Command `grep sysadmin /etc/passwd` — find lines of text `sysadmin`.**

```console
$ grep sysadmin /etc/passwd
sysadmin:x:1001:1001:System Administrator,,,,:/home/sysadmin:/bin/bash
```

This search may also match part of another field.

To search specifically for the username:

```console
$ grep '^sysadmin:' /etc/passwd
sysadmin:x:1001:1001:System Administrator,,,,:/home/sysadmin:/bin/bash
```

Parsing the template:

```text
^         → start of line
sysadmin: → exact name before delimiter
```

---

**13. `getent`: retrieving records from system databases**

General format from the chapter:

```text
getent database record
```

**Command `getent passwd sysadmin` — get user record.**

```console
$ getent passwd sysadmin
sysadmin:x:1001:1001:System Administrator,,,,:/home/sysadmin:/bin/bash
```

**Advantage over `grep /etc/passwd`:**

| `grep /etc/passwd` | `getent passwd` |
|---|---|
| Reads a specific local file | Refers to the configured system database |
| Will not find a user that exists only in an external source | Can receive a record from a connected external source |

External sources can be associated with LDAP, NIS or Active Directory - **if the corresponding integration is configured**.

There are no external users in the lab, so the result matches the local file.

**`getent` does not bypass access restrictions:** database usage `shadow` does not make protected information accessible to any user.

---

**14. `/etc/shadow`: complete analysis of nine fields**

Example for parsing:

```text
sysadmin:$6$SALT$HASH:20000:5:30:7:60:21000:
```

General format:

```text
name:password:last_change:min:max:warn:inactive:expire:reserved
```

| № | Field | Example | What does it mean? |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Username | `sysadmin` | Username |
| 2 | Password | `$6$SALT$HASH` | Password hash representation |
| 3 | Last change | `20000` | Day of last password change |
| 4 | Minimum | `5` | Minimum interval between shifts |
| 5 | Maximum | `30` | Maximum password age |
| 6 | Warn | `7` | How many days in advance to warn |
| 7 | Inactive | `60` | Period after password expiration until login is prohibited |
| 8 | Expire | `21000` | Absolute account expiration date |
| 9 | Reserved | Empty | Reserved |

**Fields 3 and 8** are expressed as the number of days from:

```text
1970-01-01 — Unix Epoch
```

**Fields 4–7** express intervals in days.

**Main difference:**

```text
last_change / expire → dates as number of days from Epoch
min / max / warn / inactive → duration
```

---

**15. Password terms: how to understand `min`, `max`, `warn`, `inactive`**

For example:

```text
last_change = 20000
min         = 5
max         = 30
warn        = 7
inactive    = 60
```

**Minimum = 5**

After a normal password change, the user must wait 5 days before the next change.

```text
min = 0 → no minimum wait
```

**Maximum = 30**

After 30 days, the password reaches its expiration date. If the login process is supported, the user must change it.

**Warn = 7**

The warning starts 7 days before the password expires.

**Inactive = 60**

Considered **after password expired**. After this period, login is prohibited and administrator intervention is required.

Simplified scale:

```text
Change password
     │
     ├─ 5 days: minimum wait until next shift
     │
     ├─ approximately 7 days before expiry: warnings
     │
     ├─ in 30 days: password has expired
     │
     └─ still 60 days: period inactive ends
```

**Inactive does not mean «user has not logged in for 60 days».**

If the password has expired, the ability to change it upon login depends on the authentication mechanism used.

**`99999` to max** — is a frequently occurring large value, approximately 274. For the practical life of the account, this is almost no regular expiration. It should not be understood as universally the maximum possible number.

**Empty field and `0` are not always equivalent in all positions.** For example, `0` in `last_change` means a requirement to change the password the next time you log in. The details are determined by the field. [Documentation `shadow`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/shadow.5.html)

---

**16. Password expiration and account expiration are not the same thing**

| Mechanism | How is it determined | What’s going on |
|---|---|---|
| Password expiration | `last_change + max` | Password change required |
| Period inactive | After password expires | After this period, login is blocked |
| Account expiration | Field `expire` | Account is no longer allowed to log in |

**Field `expire` — absolute date**, it does not count from the last password change.

For example:

```text
expire = 21000
```

means the corresponding day from 1970-01-01.

**Expiring an account does not delete it or delete the home directory.**

Source correction: simply changing the password will not necessarily fix an expired account - you need to fix the corresponding restriction.

In the source line of the chapter `expire=15050`, a `last_change=16874`. This end date already precedes the last password change; This is not an example of a normally functioning account at that time.

---

**17. Password hash, `*`, `!` and `x`**

The files use the expression «encrypted password». More precisely **password hash**, rather than reversible encryption.

Simplified:

```text
Entered password + hashing parameters
                     ↓
             result calculation
                     ↓
          comparison with saved
```

The password is not stored in clear text. However, the hash does not make a weak password invulnerable to guessing.

Example:

```text
$6$SALT$HASH
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `$6$` | SHA-512-based crypt |
| `SALT` | Salt |
| `HASH` | Calculation result |

Other formats exist; `$6$` is not required for all Linux. [Documentation `crypt`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/crypt.3.html)

**Distinguish special meanings:**

| Where and meaning | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `x` in `/etc/passwd` | Password information is listed in shadow |
| Hash in `/etc/shadow` | There is a value for checking the password |
| `*` in `/etc/shadow` | Basic password authentication is not possible |
| `!` at the beginning of the field shadow | Password locked |
| `!$6$...` | Locked field with the same hash saved |

**Password locking does not equal guaranteed disabling of all access methods.** For example, the ability to log in using the SSH- key depends on other system rules. Service processes can also continue to run.

**An empty password field should not be treated as a secure lock:** some mechanisms may allow login without a password, others prohibit it by policy.

---

**18. Why doesn’t the average user read `/etc/shadow`**

**Command `head -3 /etc/shadow` — try to read the first three lines.**

```console
$ head -3 /etc/shadow
head: cannot open '/etc/shadow' for reading: Permission denied
```

Modern explicit form of the same parameter:

```text
head -n 3 /etc/shadow
```

**Command `ls -l /etc/shadow` — see owner and rights.**

```console
$ ls -l /etc/shadow
-rw-r----- 1 root shadow 968 Nov 11 09:00 /etc/shadow
```

Parsing:

```text
- rw- r-- ---
│  │   │   └─ others: no rights
│  │   └───── group: read
│  └───────── owner: read and write
└──────────── regular file
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root` | Owner |
| `shadow` | Owning group |
| `rw-` | Owner can read and write |
| `r--` | Group can read |
| `---` | Others are not granted access |

For the rights shown, the numeric entry is **640**.

**Correction of laboratory wording:** can be read not only by the group `shadow`: the owner of root also has read permission.

**Command `sudo head -3 /etc/shadow` — read three lines with administrative rights allowed.**

```console
$ sudo head -3 /etc/shadow
[sudo] password for sysadmin:
root:$6$SALT$HASH:20000:0:99999:7:::
daemon:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
bin:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
```

**Command `tail -5 /etc/shadow` — last five lines, executed with the necessary rights.**

```console
root@localhost:~# tail -5 /etc/shadow
syslog:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
bind:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
sshd:*:20000:0:99999:7:::
operator:!:20000:0:99999:7:::
sysadmin:$6$SALT$HASH:20000:5:30:7:60:21000:
```

---

**19. System accounts**

System accounts are needed by services to perform work with limited rights.

Examples from the chapter:

```text
sshd
bind
syslog
mail
```

Idea:

```text
The service gains access to the required resources
                  ↓
She does not need to constantly work with full rights root
```

Example `/etc/passwd`:

```text
sshd:x:103:65534::/var/run/sshd:/usr/sbin/nologin
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Name | `sshd` |
| UID | `103` |
| primary group | `65534` |
| Home | `/var/run/sshd` |
| Shell | `/usr/sbin/nologin` |

**`nologin`** is intended to deny normal interactive login through this program.

Another option:

```text
/bin/false
```

Such accounts are intended for services, not for a person’s normal work.

**Source clarification:** system accounts can have existing home or work directories and own data. They don’t have to have `/home/name`.

You should not delete an account just because its name is unfamiliar: it may be required by an installed service.

---

**20. Main and supplementary groups**

A typical user process has a primary group and a list of secondary groups.

**Primary user group** is determined by the GID field in his account:

```text
sysadmin:x:1001:1001:...:/home/sysadmin:/bin/bash
                │
                └─ primary group GID 1001
```

**supplementary groups** allow you to access other resources.

Example:

```text
Main: sysadmin
Additional: adm, sudo
```

**Don’t be confused:**

```text
UID 1001 → user ID
GID 1001 → group identifier
```

The numbers may be the same, but they represent different objects.

User and group can have the same name:

```text
User sysadmin
Group sysadmin
```

This is a common organization, but not required.

The chapter mentions the historical limitation of UNIX in 16 groups. For modern Linux, this is not a universal limitation; Significantly more supplementary groups are supported.

---

**21. `/etc/group`: four fields**

Example:

```text
mail:x:12:mail,postfix
```

General format:

```text
group_name:password:GID:user_list
```

| № | Field | Meaning | Purpose |
|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Group name | `mail` | Group name |
| 2 | Password placeholder | `x` | Protected information has been removed from this file |
| 3 | GID | `12` | Group ID |
| 4 | User list | `mail,postfix` | List of explicitly listed participants |

Inside the fourth field the names are separated **with commas**, and the main fields are **colons**.

**Group passwords are rarely used.** If configured, protected data is typically located in `/etc/gshadow`.

**Important exam pitfall:**

```text
sysadmin:x:1001:
```

Empty list after last `:` **does not mean that the group has no members**.

User can have this group as primary via GID in `/etc/passwd` and not be re-written in the list `/etc/group`.

---

**22. Group viewing commands**

**Command `grep mail /etc/group` — find lines of text `mail`.**

```console
$ grep mail /etc/group
mail:x:12:mail,postfix
```

Exact group name:

```console
$ grep '^mail:' /etc/group
mail:x:12:mail,postfix
```

**Command `getent group mail` — get a group record through the system database.**

```console
$ getent group mail
mail:x:12:mail,postfix
```

**Command from the chapter `cat /etc/group | grep sysadmin` — filter the contents of the file.**

```console
$ cat /etc/group | grep sysadmin
adm:x:4:syslog,sysadmin
sudo:x:27:sysadmin
sysadmin:x:1001:
```

Here:

- `cat` outputs the file;
- `|` passes its output to the next command;
- `grep` selects rows.

The same in short:

```console
$ grep sysadmin /etc/group
adm:x:4:syslog,sysadmin
sudo:x:27:sysadmin
sysadmin:x:1001:
```

But such a search is not a universal way to get all of a user’s groups: primary membership is also determined `/etc/passwd`, and the sources can be external. More convenient for summary information `id`.

---

**23. `id`: user and groups**

**Command `id` — information about the current process.**

```console
$ id
uid=1001(sysadmin) gid=1001(sysadmin) groups=1001(sysadmin),4(adm),27(sudo)
```

| Fragment | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `uid=1001(sysadmin)` | User |
| `gid=1001(sysadmin)` | Primary/effective group in normal session |
| `groups=...` | Process groups, including main |

There are only three groups here:

```text
sysadmin
adm
sudo
```

**Command `id root` — show details of root.**

```console
$ id root
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

**This is viewing only.** Command `id root` does not switch you to root.

**Command `id -g` — output effective GID.**

```console
$ id -g
1001
```

Normally this is the primary group of the current session.

**Command `id -G` — display all GID.**

```console
$ id -G
1001 4 27
```

**Case important:**

```text
-g → one group
-G → all groups
```

Additional convenient options:

| Command | Purpose | Example output |
|---|---|---|
| `id -u` | Effective UID | `1001` |
| `id -un` | Username | `sysadmin` |
| `id -gn` | Effective group name | `sysadmin` |
| `id -Gn` | All group names | `sysadmin adm sudo` |

`-n` replaces numeric identifiers with names.

**Accuracy:** without name `id` shows the current process data; with name—data of the specified account. After changing groups, an already open session will not necessarily receive the new list immediately. [Documentation `id`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/id.1.html)

---

**24. `man 5 passwd`: why do we need the number 5**

**Command `man 5 passwd` — open format description `/etc/passwd`.**

```console
$ man 5 passwd
PASSWD(5)                 File Formats                 PASSWD(5)

NAME
       passwd - the password file

DESCRIPTION
       /etc/passwd contains one line for each user account,
       with seven fields delimited by colons.
```

Here:

```text
5 → directory section on file formats
```

Name `passwd` is used for both the command and the file format.

| Designation | What it describes |
|---|---|
| `passwd(1)` | Password change command |
| `passwd(5)` | Accounts file format |

Therefore `man 5 passwd` definitely opens the right page.

**Keys in the help viewer:**

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| `Enter` | Next line |
| `Space` | Next page |
| `/text` | Search |
| `n` | Next match |
| `q` | Exit |

---

**25. `who`: who is currently logged in**

**Command `who` — show logged current sessions.**

```console
$ who
root     tty2  2026-11-11 10:00
sysadmin tty1  2026-11-11 09:58 (:0)
sysadmin pts/0 2026-11-11 09:59 (:0.0)
sysadmin pts/1 2026-11-11 10:00 (192.168.1.10)
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `root`, `sysadmin` | Logged in user name |
| `tty2`, `pts/0` | Terminal |
| Date and time | Start of session |
| Value in brackets | Input source if recorded |

**Terminals:**

| View | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tty1`, `tty2` | Usually local text consoles |
| `pts/0`, `pts/1` | Pseudo-terminals |
| `console` | Console in the appropriate environment |

**`pts` does not necessarily mean SSH.** The pseudo-terminal can also be used by a local graphic terminal.

Sources in the example:

```text
(:0), (:0.0)      → local graphic display designations
(192.168.1.10)    → remote login source address
```

One user can have multiple sessions, so multiple lines `sysadmin` — normal situation.

**Important:** `who` shows session recordings. Not every open terminal is necessarily registered in the database used.

After `su -` command `id` may show root, and `who` — the original user of the session. They answer different questions.

---

**26. `who -b`, `who -r`: loading and runlevel**

**Command `who -b` — show last download time.**

```console
$ who -b
         system boot  2026-11-11 09:00
```

**Command `who -r` — show the current runlevel and the time it was installed.**

```console
$ who -r
         run-level 5  2026-11-11 09:01
```

**Combination from the chapter:**

```console
$ who -b -r
         system boot  2026-11-11 09:00
         run-level 5  2026-11-11 09:01
```

**Runlevel** — system operation level in the traditional model SysV init.

For this chapter, the main thing to remember is:

```text
-b → boot
-r → runlevel
```

The output depends on the availability of corresponding entries and the initialization system used. [Documentation `who`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/who.1.html)

---

**27. `w`: who is logged in and what they are doing**

**Command `w` — detailed information about current sessions and system status.**

```console
$ w
10:44:03 up 1:44, 3 users, load average: 0.78, 0.44, 0.19
USER     TTY   FROM          LOGIN@ IDLE  JCPU  PCPU WHAT
root     tty2  -            10:00  43:44 0.01s 0.01s -bash
sysadmin pts/0 :0.0         09:59  0.00s 0.14s 0.13s ssh 192.168.1.2
sysadmin pts/1 192.168.1.10  10:00  0.00s 0.03s 0.01s w
```

**First line:**

| Meaning | Field value |
|---|---|
| `10:44:03` | Current time |
| `up 1:44` | System running 1 hour 44 minutes |
| `3 users` | Number of sessions counted |
| `0.78, 0.44, 0.19` | Load average for 1, 5 and 15 minutes |

Multiple sessions can belong to one person.

**Columns:**

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `USER` | Session user |
| `TTY` | Terminal |
| `FROM` | Input source |
| `LOGIN@` | Login time |
| `IDLE` | Idle Time Estimation |
| `JCPU` | Processor time of processes associated with the terminal |
| `PCPU` | CPU time of the current process from `WHAT` |
| `WHAT` | Current command |

**Laboratory correction:** `JCPU` — not just background jobs. It includes processes associated with the terminal, including running background jobs; Previously completed background jobs are not included in this indicator. [Documentation `w`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/w.1.html)

`0.13s` means 0,13 seconds of CPU- time.

**Load average is not equal to the percentage CPU.** It takes into account running/ready tasks and uninterruptible sleep tasks. Comparison with quantity CPU is only a guide and not an exact conversion to percentage.

---

**28. `last`: entry and exit history**

**Command `last` — show logged session history.**

```console
$ last
sysadmin pts/1 192.168.1.10 Wed Nov 11 10:00   still logged in
sysadmin pts/0 :0.0         Wed Nov 11 09:59 - 10:20  (00:21)
root     tty2              Wed Nov 11 09:30 - 09:45  (00:15)
reboot   system boot 6.8.0  Wed Nov 11 09:00   still running

wtmp begins Wed Nov 11 09:00:00 2026
```

Usually newer entries are displayed first.

| Fragment | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `sysadmin` | User |
| `pts/1` | Terminal |
| `192.168.1.10` | Input source |
| `10:00` | Login time |
| `09:59 - 10:20` | Start and end of session |
| `(00:21)` | Duration |
| `still logged in` | There is no end to this session in the log |
| `reboot` | System boot record |
| `wtmp begins` | Start of available file data |

In the record `reboot` the kernel version may be displayed at the source location.

**Main source in the material:**

```text
/var/log/wtmp
```

This is a binary log, so it is read through `last`, and not normal `cat`.

**History limited to available records:** it does not necessarily cover the entire lifetime of the machine - the file may be missing, cleared, or rotated. [Documentation `last`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/last.1@@util-linux.html)

---

**29. `utmp`, `wtmp` and difference `who`, `w`, `last`**

| Source | What reflects | Basic Commands |
|---|---|---|
| `utmp` | Current logged sessions | `who`, traditional `w` |
| `wtmp` | History of inputs, outputs and system events | `last` |

**Source correction:** normal path `utmp` — **`/var/run/utmp`**, often corresponding `/run/utmp`, and not `/var/log/utmp`. Used for history `/var/log/wtmp`. [Format documentation](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/utmp.5.html)

Modern tool implementations may use other session sources.

**Main comparison:**

| Command | What question does it answer? |
|---|---|
| `id` | What are the IDs and groups of the current process or specified user? |
| `who` | What sessions are currently logged in? |
| `w` | What sessions are active and what are their users doing? |
| `last` | What inputs and outputs are recorded in history? |

**Another inaccuracy of the chapter:** `who` also shows the entry time. Difference `last` — primarily in the presence of a history of completed sessions and duration, and not just the login date.

`last` is not a command to view failed login attempts. For this purpose, the corresponding systems use `lastb` and log `btmp`, discussed in the previous chapter.

---

**30. What you need to be able to do from the laboratory**

| Task | Command | Expected result |
|---|---|---|
| Go to root | `su -` | After authentication, the root shell opens |
| Check identity | `id` | `uid=0(root)` |
| Return | `exit` | The prompt is returned `sysadmin` |
| Check regular user | `id` | `uid=1001(sysadmin)` in the laboratory |
| Try reading shadow | `head /etc/shadow` | `Permission denied` |
| Read with permissions | `sudo head /etc/shadow` | Display protected records |
| View users | `head /etc/passwd` | First 10 lines |
| Find entry | `grep '^sysadmin:' /etc/passwd` | Record sysadmin |
| View rights shadow | `ls -l /etc/shadow` | Owner, Group and Permissions |
| Retrieve record via database | `getent passwd sysadmin` | User string |
| Open file format | `man 5 passwd` | Description of the seven fields |
| Check another user | `id root` | Information about root without switching |
| View sessions | `who` | User, terminal, time, source |
| View activity | `w` | Sessions, commands, system summary |
| View history | `last` | Entries from login history |

---

**31. Common exam pitfalls**

| Incorrect statement | Correct |
|---|---|
| In `/etc/passwd` there are open passwords | Usually there `x`, hashes are moved to shadow |
| `x` means locked password | In passwd this is a pointer to shadow |
| `sudo` asks for password root | Typically the calling user’s password |
| `su` always switches only to root | You can specify another user |
| `su` and `su -` are completely the same | Environment preparation and directory differ |
| After `sudo` all commands become root | Only those explicitly launched with the necessary rights |
| Timeout sudo terminates program | Typically this is the authentication cache period |
| `id root` makes user root | This is viewing only |
| GID in passwd - supplementary group | This is the primary group |
| Empty list `/etc/group` means no participants | Main participants can be defined via passwd |
| `id -G` shows only supplementary groups | Main and additional |
| `inactive=60` — 60 days without login | 60 days after password expiration |
| `expire=30` — account is still alive 30 days | This is the absolute day from Epoch |
| Changing the password removes any account restrictions | Account expiration date - separate restriction |
| `JCPU` — background processes only | Processes associated with the terminal |
| `pts/0` necessarily means remote login | This is a pseudo-terminal, local is also possible |
| `who` shows all existing users | Shows currently logged sessions |
| `last` shows all failed login attempts | He is reading a story from wtmp |
| Load average — exact percentage CPU | This is a different indicator |

---

**32. Self-check Questions — with Answers**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is UID for root? | `0` |
| What three types of users does the chapter cover? | Root, regular, system |
| What are system accounts for? | For services and background processes |
| What does UID mean? | User ID |
| What does GID mean? | Group ID |
| Where is general information about local users? | `/etc/passwd` |
| How many fields are there in passwd? | 7 |
| How are the fields separated? | Colons |
| Where are the password hashes and timing? | `/etc/shadow` |
| How many fields are there in shadow? | 9 |
| Where are local groups defined? | `/etc/group` |
| How many fields are there in group? | 4 |
| Where is the group’s protected information? | `/etc/gshadow` |
| What does it mean? `x` to passwd? | Used by shadow |
| Which field passwd contains UID? | Third |
| Which field contains the primary group? | Fourth |
| Which field contains the home directory? | Sixth |
| Which field contains the shell? | Seventh |
| What is GECOS? | Information field/comment |
| Where is the home directory of root? | Usually `/root` |
| What does it mean? `/usr/sbin/nologin`? | Regular Interactive Login Denial Program |
| From what date are days shadow counted? | With 1970-01-01 |
| What is minimum? | Minimum interval between password changes |
| What is maximum? | Maximum password age |
| What is warn? | Warning period before password expires |
| What is inactive? | Period after password expiration until login is prohibited |
| What is expire? | Absolute account expiration date |
| Is an expired account automatically deleted? | No |
| What does it mean? `!` at the beginning of the password field? | Password locked |
| What does it mean? `*` instead of hash? | Cannot authenticate with regular UNIX- password |
| How to open login shell root? | `su -` |
| How to get to bob? | `su - bob` |
| Whose password is usually needed for `su - bob`? | Bob |
| Whose password is usually needed for sudo? | Caller |
| How to return after su? | `exit` |
| How to check current IDs? | `id` |
| How to view root data without switching? | `id root` |
| What does it do? `id -g`? | Outputs effective GID |
| What does it do? `id -G`? | Displays all GID |
| How to get a user record from the system database? | `getent passwd name` |
| How to get a group entry? | `getent group name` |
| How is getent wider than the local file grep? | Can use configured external sources |
| How can I see the first three lines? | `head -n 3 file` |
| How to see the last five? | `tail -n 5 file` |
| How to view the rights of shadow? | `ls -l /etc/shadow` |
| What does it mean? `-rw-r-----`? | The owner reads/writes, the group reads, the rest have no rights |
| How to open the description of passwd as a file? | `man 5 passwd` |
| Who shows current sessions? | `who` |
| Who shows sessions and running commands? | `w` |
| Who shows login history? | `last` |
| What does it do? `who -b`? | Shows loading time |
| What does it do? `who -r`? | Shows runlevel |
| What does it mean? `PCPU`? | CPU-time of the current process from WHAT |
| What does it mean? `JCPU`? | CPU-time of processes associated with the terminal |
| What are the intervals of load average? | 1, 5 and 15 minutes |
| Where is the login history? | `/var/log/wtmp` |
| What does it mean? `still logged in`? | No output recorded for session |
| What does it mean? `reboot` to last? | System boot record |

**First of all, learn three formats - `passwd`, `shadow`, `group`; differences `su`/`sudo`; parameters `id -g`/`id -G`; and destination `who`, `w`, `last`.** This is the basis of the entire chapter and lab.

title: Creating Users and Groups
summary: useradd, groupadd, passwords and account management
markdown:
Read completely **chapter 16 and laboratory 16**. Below is a summary of all educational content: creating and changing users and groups, default settings, passwords, expiration dates and deleting accounts.

**All output examples are educational.** UID, GID, shells and directory permissions are system dependent. I did not run the commands from the documents.

**User creation examples `jane` — individual options**, rather than a sequence to execute multiple times: re-creating an existing user will fail. The sequence of the laboratory itself is given separately.

---

**1. What you need to know for the exam**

The topic is indicated in the chapter **5.2 — Creating Users and Groups**, weight - **2**.

Basic skills:

- create, rename and delete groups;
- create users;
- set UID, main and supplementary groups;
- create home directory and copy initial files;
- understand `/etc/default/useradd`, `/etc/login.defs`, `/etc/skel`;
- set and change passwords;
- manage deadlines via `chage`;
- change user via `usermod`;
- distinguish between password blocking and account deletion;
- understand the consequences of changing UID/GID.

Main commands:

```text
groupadd
groupmod
groupdel
useradd
passwd
chage
usermod
userdel
```

---

**2. Why are separate users and groups needed?**

A separate account for each person allows you to:

- grant different rights;
- have a separate home directory;
- assign groups individually;
- issue administrative powers through `sudo`;
- associate log activities with a specific user.

**Group** is convenient for sharing.

Example:

```text
Users jane and bob are members of research.
The project directory belongs to the group research.
The group has been granted the necessary rights.
→ Both users can work with the project.
```

**Creating a group does not automatically grant access.** The group must be associated with files or directories and assigned the appropriate permissions.

Convenient operating procedure:

```text
1. Schedule users and groups.
2. Create groups.
3. Create users with the required memberships.
4. Set passwords.
5. Check the result.
```

---

**3. What files are involved**

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/etc/passwd` | General information about local users |
| `/etc/shadow` | Password hashes and expiration dates |
| `/etc/group` | Groups and lists of additional participants |
| `/etc/gshadow` | Protected group information |
| `/etc/default/useradd` | Part of the user creation settings |
| `/etc/login.defs` | Additional settings for account management tools |
| `/etc/skel` | Home directory initial content templates |
| `/home/name` | Typical home directory location |
| `/var/mail` or `/var/spool/mail` | Possible local mailbox locations |

Brief repetition of formats from chapter 15:

```text
/etc/passwd:
name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell

/etc/group:
group_name:x:GID:user_list

/etc/shadow:
name:hash:last_change:min:max:warn:inactive:expire:reserved
```

Special commands are used to manage accounts. Manual editing of these databases easily leads to inconsistent records.

---

**4. UID, GID and User Private Group**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| UID | User ID |
| GID | Group ID |
| Primary group | primary group |
| Supplementary groups | supplementary groups |
| UPG — User Private Group | A separate group created for the user |

Example UPG:

```text
User: jane
Group: jane
```

The user may be able to:

```text
UID 1002
Main GID 1002
```

But **matching UID and GID is not a requirement of Linux**.

If UPG is not created, the primary group can be selected from the settings, for example `users`.

**UID `0` means administrative identity root.**

The ranges of the remaining UID/GID depend on the settings:

- in old examples, regular accounts start with `500`;
- in many systems - with `1000`;
- system accounts are usually allocated a separate range.

`60000` in the source is an example of an administrative boundary, and not a universal technical limit Linux.

**On multiple machines, the same name does not guarantee the same identity:** when sharing files, consistent UID/GID is important. A centralized account system helps maintain such compliance.

---

**5. Administrative rights for the laboratory**

Creating and changing local accounts usually requires root or appropriate permissions through `sudo`.

**Command `su -` — open shell root.**

```console
sysadmin@localhost:~$ su -
Password:
root@localhost:~#
```

In the training virtual machine, the password is root:

```text
netlab123
```

Check:

```console
root@localhost:~# id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

In further examples:

```text
# → command executed with administrative rights
$ → normal user
```

You do not need to enter a prompt character.

Most account change commands **if successful, do not print anything**. Therefore, after them they are usually checked through `getent`, `id`, `grep` or `ls`.

---

**6. `groupadd`: group creation**

General syntax:

```text
groupadd [parameters] name_group
```

**Command `groupadd -g 1005 research` — create a group with the specified GID.**

```console
# groupadd -g 1005 research
# getent group research
research:x:1005:
```

Parsing:

```text
-g 1005 → GID new group
research → name
```

An empty last field means there are no additional participants explicitly listed.

**Command `groupadd development` — create a group with GID automatically selected.**

```console
# groupadd development
# getent group development
development:x:1006:
```

`1006` — is a possible result, not a required value.

Automatic selection takes into account ranges and already occupied identifiers. The rule from the chapter should not be understood as «maximum GID in general in the system plus one» without taking into account the settings. [Documentation `groupadd`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/groupadd.8.html)

---

**7. `groupadd -r`: system group**

**Command `groupadd -r sales` — create a group from the system range GID.**

```console
# groupadd -r sales
# getent group sales
sales:x:999:
```

In the laboratory:

```console
# groupadd -r research
# groupadd -r sales
# getent group research
research:x:999:
# getent group sales
sales:x:998:
```

Specific values ​​may vary.

**`-r` means system group**, rather than a special set of file permissions.

Such a group:

- gets an identifier from the corresponding system range;
- does not automatically become administrative;
- does not access all files.

---

**8. User and group names**

Portability recommendations from the chapter:

- start with a small Latin letter or `_`;
- use letters, numbers, `_`, `-`;
- do not start or end a name with a hyphen;
- choose short, clear names.

Examples:

```text
research
sales
project_team
student
jane
```

The chapter talks about a common limit of 32 characters and a more conservative choice of up to 16 characters.

**These are portability guidelines, not rules that are the same for all implementations.** Real limits are checked by specific tools.

Case has the meaning:

```text
jane ≠ Jane
```

In the source material there are `Jane` instead `jane` and `/test/Jane` instead `/test/jane`. This does not automatically count as a single user or directory.

---

**9. `groupmod -n`: group rename**

General format:

```text
groupmod -n new_name old_name
```

**Command `groupmod -n clerks sales` — rename sales to clerks.**

```console
# groupmod -n clerks sales
# getent group clerks
clerks:x:999:
```

**GID is saved.**

Before:

```console
# ls -l index.html
-rw-r----- 1 root sales 0 Nov 11 10:00 index.html
```

After:

```console
# ls -l index.html
-rw-r----- 1 root clerks 0 Nov 11 10:00 index.html
```

The file stores GID, so the new name of the same group is displayed.

**Renaming a group does not create a new number group.**

At the same time, application settings or scripts where the old name is written in text may require separate changes.

---

**10. `groupmod -g`: change GID and «orphaned» files**

**Command `groupmod -g 10003 clerks` — change GID group.**

```console
# groupmod -g 10003 clerks
# getent group clerks
clerks:x:10003:
```

Previously the file belonged to GID `999`.

After changing a group entry, the file will not necessarily receive a new GID:

```console
# ls -l index.html
-rw-r----- 1 root 999 0 Nov 11 10:00 index.html
```

Number `999` instead of name means that no matching group name was found for it.

**Orphaned file — «orphaned» file:** file with UID or GID that no longer has a corresponding user or group entry.

**Command `find / -nogroup` — find files without a recognized group.**

```console
# find / -nogroup
/root/index.html
/srv/project/report.txt
```

The command only searches, does not delete anything.

**Clarification:** if the old GID already matches another group, the file will be displayed with its name. He doesn’t have to remain nameless.

Modern `groupmod` updates the primary group of users who used it, but **ownership of files with old GID needs to be checked and corrected separately**. [Documentation `groupmod`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/groupmod.8.html)

---

**11. `groupdel`: delete group**

**16. Home directory, `UMASK` and `/etc/skel`**

**Write path to `/etc/passwd` and creating a directory are different actions.**

May exist:

```text
jane:x:1008:1008::/home/jane:/bin/sh
```

but the `/home/jane` is not yet on the disk.

When creating a new home directory, copies of them may appear in:

```text
/home/jane/
```

**20. `-b`, `-d`, `-k`, `-s`, `-c`: differences**

**`-b` specifies the stem to which the name is appended.**

```console
# useradd -m -b /test jane
# getent passwd jane
jane:x:1009:1009::/test/jane:/bin/sh
```

**`-d` specifies a ready-made full path.**

```console
# useradd -m -d /srv/jane-home jane
# getent passwd jane
jane:x:1009:1009::/srv/jane-home:/bin/sh
```

Comparison:

```text
-b /test         → /test/jane
-d /srv/jane-home → /srv/jane-home
```

`-d` does not by itself guarantee directory creation; used for this `-m`.

**`-k` specifies the source of the initial files.**

Example from the chapter:

```console
# useradd -m -k /home/sysadmin jane
# ls /home/jane
Desktop Documents Downloads Music Pictures Public Templates Videos
```

In this example, the content `/home/sysadmin` is used as a template and copied. These are individual copies, not links to a shared directory.

For the intended use `-k` required `-m`.

**`-s` specifies the shell.**

```console
# useradd -s /bin/bash jane
# getent passwd jane
jane:x:1009:1009::/home/jane:/bin/bash
```

**`-c` sets a comment.**

```console
# useradd -c 'Jane Doe' jane
# getent passwd jane
jane:x:1009:1009:Jane Doe:/home/jane:/bin/sh
```

Quotes are preserved `Jane Doe` with one argument.

Additionally, for the explicit creation of UPG there is `-U`, to refuse it - `-N`. The default behavior depends on the settings. [Documentation `useradd`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/useradd.8.html)

**23. What to know about password quality and duration**

The chapter discusses:

- length;
- composition;
- disclosure protection;
- expiration date;
- disadvantages of too frequent mandatory changes.

For the exam, you need to understand which settings are responsible for timing and warnings.

**Practical clarifications to the old text:**

- a long unique passphrase can be convenient and stable;
- personal information and predictable patterns are poor foundations;
- a required character mix does not in itself guarantee persistence;
- change every 30/60/90 days is not a universal modern recommendation;
- changing the password does not guarantee that an attacker’s already established session will be disconnected.

Modern recommendations NIST do not require arbitrary periodic changes without signs of compromise and do not require mandatory mixing of character types. **This is a clarification of practice; appointment `chage` and the term fields still need to be known.** [NIST SP 800-63B](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html)

**30. `usermod -L` and `-U`: password lock**

**Command `usermod -L student` — block password.**

Before:

```text
student:$6$SALT$HASH:20768:0:99999:7:30::
```

After:

```console
# usermod -L student
# getent shadow student
student:!$6$SALT$HASH:20768:0:99999:7:30::
```

Added to the beginning of the password field `!`.

**Command `usermod -U student` — remove such lock.**

```console
# usermod -U student
# getent shadow student
student:$6$SALT$HASH:20768:0:99999:7:30::
```

**Key source fix:** `-L` blocks **password**, rather than guaranteeing all access methods.

This is optional:

- prohibits entry using the SSH- key;
- terminates already running processes;
- closes existing sessions;
- sets the account expiration date.

If no password was initially set, simply unlocking does not create a new working password.
