Removing a group with the same name depends on the settings and use of the group by other users.

In particular, `USERGROUPS_ENAB=yes` may allow automatic removal of unnecessary UPG. [Documentation `userdel`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/userdel.8.html)

**Deleting an account and blocking a password are different operations.** When locked, the entry and numeric identity are preserved.

---

**33. Why reusing UID/GID matters**

Let’s say:

```text
jane had UID 1009.
Account deleted.
File /srv/report.txt remains with UID 1009.
```

If another user later receives UID `1009`, the file may appear as owned by it and be granted the appropriate rights.

The same applies to GID.

Therefore, it is important to remember:

> Files belong to numeric identifiers, and names are the result of their comparison with the account database.

This explains the consequences:

- rename;
- changes UID/GID;
- delete;
- reassigning identifiers.

---

**34. The entire laboratory sequence**

Below is a connected sequence from Lab 16. This is a training scenario that involves deleting a created account.

| Step | Command or action | Result |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | `su -` | Shell root |
| 2 | `groupadd -r research` | New system group |
| 3 | `groupadd -r sales` | Second group |
| 4 | `getent group research` | For example `research:x:999:` |
| 5 | `grep '^sales:' /etc/group` | For example `sales:x:998:` |
| 6 | `groupmod -n clerks sales` | Renaming |
| 7 | `groupmod -g 10003 clerks` | New GID |
| 8 | `groupdel clerks` | Delete a group |
| 9 | `useradd -D` | View defaults |
| 10 | `useradd -D -f 30` | New INACTIVE for future accounts |
| 11 | `nano /etc/default/useradd` | Install `CREATE_MAIL_SPOOL=yes` |
| 12 | `useradd -G research -c 'Linux Student' -m student` | Create student |
| 13 | `usermod -aG research sysadmin` | Add sysadmin to research |
| 14 | `getent group research` | Both additional participants |
| 15 | `getent passwd student` | General entry |
| 16 | `getent shadow student` | Before setting the password field `!` |
| 17 | `passwd student` | Setting a training password |
| 18 | `getent shadow student` | The hash is now present |
| 19 | `last student` | History check |
| 20 | `userdel -r student` | Deleting account, home and mail |

**Key creation step:**

```console
# useradd -G research -c 'Linux Student' -m student
# getent passwd student
student:x:1002:1002:Linux Student:/home/student:/bin/sh
```

At UPG:

```console
# getent group student
student:x:1002:
```

supplementary group after adding sysadmin:

```console
# getent group research
research:x:999:student,sysadmin
```

**It is better to check account deletion through:**

```console
# getent passwd student
#
```

Check only `/etc/group`, as at the end of the lab, checks group records rather than directly the existence of the user.

---

**35. Top exam pitfalls**

| Error | Correct |
|---|---|
| `groupadd` adds a user to a group | Creates a group |
| `groupmod -n` changes GID | Changes name |
| `groupmod -g` changes name | Changes GID |
| `groupdel` deletes group files | Deletes a group entry |
| `useradd` always creates home | Depends on `-m`, `-M` and settings |
| `useradd` immediately sets the password | Usually the password is set separately |
| `-g` and `-G` are the same | Main and supplementary groups |
| `-m` and `-M` are the same | Create and do not create home |
| `-b` specifies the full path home | Specifies the stem to which the name is appended |
| `-d` automatically transfers files | Changes path; transfer through `usermod -m` |
| `/etc/skel` updates all users | Used when creating initial content |
| `useradd -D` changes existing accounts | Views/changes defaults |
| `usermod -G` always adds | Typically replaces a list |
| `usermod -aG` replaces list | Adds to it |
| Changing groups immediately changes all processes | Usually a new session is needed |
| `usermod -L` denies any access | Locks the password |
| `chage -E` sets the password duration | Sets the account expiration date |
| `chage -M` sets the account expiration date | Sets the maximum password age |
| Inactive — days without entry | Days after password expires |
| `userdel -r` deletes all files on the system | Home and mail; other files may remain |
| Renaming the user changes UID | UID is saved |
| Absence `last student` proves that there was never an entry | Only no entry in the viewed history |

---

**36. Self-check Questions — with Answers**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Which team creates the group? | `groupadd` |
| How to set GID when creating? | `groupadd -g GID name` |
| What does it mean? `groupadd -r`? | System group |
| How to rename a group? | `groupmod -n new old` |
| How to change GID? | `groupmod -g GID group` |
| How to delete a group? | `groupdel group` |
| Why does renaming usually preserve file access? | GID remains the same |
| Does groupmod GID change all files automatically? | No |
| How to find files without a recognized group? | `find / -nogroup` |
| What is UPG? | Separate group for user |
| Do UID and GID have to match? | No |
| Which command creates a user? | `useradd` |
| How to view defaults? | `useradd -D` |
| Where is part defaults stored? | `/etc/default/useradd` |
| Where are the UID/GID ranges and other settings? | `/etc/login.defs` |
| Where are the home file templates? | `/etc/skel` |
| What does it do? `useradd -D -f 30`? | Changes INACTIVE for future users |
| Does this automatically apply to older accounts? | No |
| What does it mean? `CREATE_MAIL_SPOOL=yes`? | Create local mailbox |
| How to set UID? | `-u` |
| How to set the primary group? | `-g` |
| How to set supplementary groups? | `-G` |
| What separates the groups in the list? | Commas |
| How to request the creation of home? | `-m` |
| How to prevent its creation? | `-M` |
| What does this set `-b`? | Base directory |
| What does this set `-d`? | Full path home |
| What does this set `-k`? | Template directory |
| What is required with `-k` in the chapter examples? | `-m` |
| How to set shell? | `-s` |
| How to set GECOS? | `-c` |
| How to set the password student from root? | `passwd student` |
| How do I change my own password? | `passwd` |
| Why is nothing visible when I type? | Terminal hides input |
| What does it mean? `!` after the usual useradd? | Password not set/locked |
| Which team manages deadlines? | `chage` |
| How can I see the deadlines? | `chage -l name` |
| How to set the maximum 60 days? | `chage -M 60 name` |
| How to set the minimum 5 days? | `chage -m 5 name` |
| How to set a warning for 7 days? | `chage -W 7 name` |
| How to set inactive? | `chage -I days name` |
| How do I set the account expiration date? | `chage -E date name` |
| How do I request a change the next time I log in? | `chage -d 0 name` |
| Which command changes an existing user? | `usermod` |
| How to add a group without losing old ones? | `usermod -aG group user` |
| What does it do? `usermod -G` without `-a`? | Replaces the list of supplementary groups |
| How to rename a user? | `usermod -l new old` |
| Will home be renamed automatically? | No |
| How to transfer home? | `usermod -d new_path -m user` |
| How to block a password? | `usermod -L user` |
| How to unlock? | `usermod -U user` |
| How to delete an account while keeping home? | `userdel user` |
| How to delete along with home and mail? | `userdel -r user` |
| Will the files remain outside home? | May stay |
| How to view the history of a specific user? | `last name` |
| How can I view failed logins? | `lastb` |
| How to check the existence of a user? | `getent passwd name` |
| How to check user groups? | `id name` |

**First of all, learn:** `-g`/`-G`, `-m`/`-M`, `-G`/`-aG`, `useradd -D`, destination `/etc/skel`, parameters `chage` and the differences between locking a password, deleting an account, and deleting its files.

title: Ownership and Permissions
summary: rwx, chmod, chown, directories and umask
markdown:
Read completely **chapter 17 and laboratory 17**. Below is a full summary: file ownership, rights `rwx`, working with directories, `chmod`, `chown`, `chgrp`, `newgrp`, `umask`, all six situations from the chapter and the laboratory sequence.

**Output examples are educational.** Owners, dates and initial rights may vary. I did not run the commands from the documents.

The main analysis relates to the usual Linux rights model: **owner → group → others**. Additional mechanisms such as ACL and special bits may influence the result; necessary exceptions are noted below.

---

**1. What you need to know for the exam**

Topic from file: **5.3 — Managing File Permissions and Ownership**, weight - **2**.

You need to be able to:

- read output `ls -l`;
- determine the owner and group of the file;
- distinguish between file and directory rights;
- select which three rights apply to the user;
- consider directories along the file path;
- change rights in symbolic and numeric ways;
- change owner and group;
- understand temporary group switching through `newgrp`;
- calculate initial rights via `umask`.

Main commands:

```text
ls
stat
id
groups
newgrp
chgrp
chown
chmod
umask
```

---

**2. The file has two owners**

Each file and directory has:

| Type of ownership | Meaning |
|---|---|
| User owner | File owner |
| Group owner | Owning group |

Example:

```text
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin research 0 Nov 11 10:00 report.txt
              │        │
              │        └─ group
              └────────── user
```

Within a file system, ownership is related to:

```text
UID → user ID
GID → group identifier
```

Names are displayed after matching these numbers with the user and group databases.

If no name is found for UID/GID, you can see the number:

```text
-rw-r----- 1 1009 1005 120 Nov 11 10:00 report.txt
```

**Renaming a user or group does not change the numeric owner of the file.** Changing UID/GID or deleting an entry may leave files with the same IDs.

---

**3. Who owns the new file**

In the normal case, the new file receives:

- owner user - the user of the creating process;
- group - the current effective group of the process, usually its primary group.

**Command `touch /tmp/filetest1` — create a new empty file.**

```console
$ touch /tmp/filetest1
$ ls -l /tmp/filetest1
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 /tmp/filetest1
```

If the file already exists, `touch` usually updates its timestamps rather than clearing the contents.

**Exception:** when setgid is installed on the parent directory, the new file can inherit the directory group. Therefore the rule «is always the primary group of the creator» is not universal. [File Attribute Documentation](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/inode.7.html)

---

**4. `ls -l`: how to read a string**

**Command `ls -l report.txt` — detailed information about the file.**

```console
$ ls -l report.txt
-rw-r----- 1 sysadmin research 120 Nov 11 10:00 report.txt
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-` | Type: regular file |
| `rw-r-----` | Nine regular permission bits |
| `1` | Number of hard links |
| `sysadmin` | Owner |
| `research` | Group |
| `120` | Size in bytes |
| `Nov 11 10:00` | Content change time |
| `report.txt` | Name |

First ten characters:

```text
- rw- r-- ---
│  │   │   └─ others
│  │   └───── group
│  └───────── owner
└──────────── file type
```

**The first character is not an access right.**

After these characters there are sometimes additional markers, for example `.` or `+`. They are not another common law `rwx`.

---

**5. File types**

| First character | Type | What does it mean? |
|---|---|---|
| `-` | Regular file | Text, program, data, empty file |
| `d` | Directory | Contains names and references to objects |
| `l` | Symbolic link | Points to a different path |
| `b` | Block device | Block device interface |
| `c` | Character device | Character device interface |
| `p` | Named pipe - FIFO | Communication between processes |
| `s` | Socket | Interprocess communication |

Most often encountered in normal work:

```text
-  d  l
```

Special devices are often located in `/dev`; sockets and FIFO may be located in other directories.

---

**6. Useful options `ls`**

| Command | Purpose | Example output |
|---|---|---|
| `ls -l file` | File details | `-rw-r--r-- 1 alice users ... file` |
| `ls -l directory` | Detailed list of contents | Lines of files inside a directory |
| `ls -ld directory` | Information about the directory itself | `drwxr-xr-x 2 alice users ... directory` |
| `ls -a` | Names, including hidden ones | `. .. .bashrc report.txt` |
| `ls -la` | Detailed list with hidden | Rights, owners and names of all entries |

**Don’t be confused:**

```text
ls -l priv-dir  → contents priv-dir
ls -ld priv-dir → priv-dir itself
```

Example:

```console
$ ls -ld priv-dir
drwxrwx--- 2 sysadmin sysadmin 4096 Nov 11 10:00 priv-dir
```

**Hidden names begin with a dot:**

```text
.bashrc
.profile
.cache
```

```text
.  → current directory
.. → parent directory
```

Hidden name **is not a protection mechanism**. Normal rights apply to him.

---

**7. `id` and `groups`: who are you and what groups are available**

**Command `id` — IDs and groups of the current process.**

```console
$ id
uid=1001(sysadmin) gid=1001(sysadmin) groups=1001(sysadmin),4(adm),27(sudo),1005(research),1006(development)
```

| Fragment | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `uid=1001(sysadmin)` | User |
| `gid=1001(sysadmin)` | Current Primary/Effective Group |
| `groups=...` | Available groups |

**Command `groups` — display group names.**

```console
$ groups
sysadmin adm sudo research development
```

`id` is more convenient for checking the current GID, `groups` — for a short list of memberships.

---

**8. `newgrp`: temporarily change current group**

**Command `newgrp research` — open a shell with the current group research.**

Before:

```console
$ id
uid=1001(sysadmin) gid=1001(sysadmin) groups=1001(sysadmin),1005(research),1006(development)
```

Switching:

```console
$ newgrp research
$ id
uid=1001(sysadmin) gid=1005(research) groups=1005(research),1001(sysadmin),1006(development)
```

Now the new file in the normal directory gets group research:

```console
$ touch /tmp/filetest2
$ ls -l /tmp/filetest2
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin research 0 Nov 11 10:05 /tmp/filetest2
```

**Username has not changed.** The group of the current shell has changed.

**Command `exit` — exit this shell.**

```console
$ exit
exit
$ id
uid=1001(sysadmin) gid=1001(sysadmin) groups=1001(sysadmin),1005(research),1006(development)
```

**Comparison:**

| Command | What changes |
|---|---|
| `newgrp research` | Current group of the new shell |
| `usermod -g research sysadmin` | primary group in the account |
| `chgrp research file` | Group of a specific file |

For permanent change via `usermod` requires administrative rights.

---

**9. `chgrp`: change group of existing file**

General syntax:

```text
chgrp group file
```

**Command `chgrp research sample` — assign group research to the file.**

```console
$ ls -l sample
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 sample

$ chgrp research sample
$ ls -l sample
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin research 0 Nov 11 10:00 sample
```

**A regular user can change the group if:**

1. he owns the file;
2. the target group is available to him by membership.

Administrative rights allow you to do more.

Example of refusal:

```console
$ chgrp development /etc/passwd
chgrp: changing group of '/etc/passwd': Operation not permitted
```

Membership `development` does not make the user the owner `/etc/passwd`.

---

**10. `chgrp -R`: recursive group change**

**Command `chgrp -R development test_dir` — change the group of the directory and its contents.**

```console
$ chgrp -R development test_dir
$
```

On success there is usually no separate output.

Check:

```console
$ ls -ld test_dir
drwxrwx--- 2 sysadmin development 4096 Nov 11 10:00 test_dir

$ ls -l test_dir
total 0
-rw-r----- 1 sysadmin development 0 Nov 11 10:00 report.txt
```

**`-R` — recursive:** the directory itself, subdirectories and files are affected.

Without `-R`:

```text
chgrp development test_dir
```

changes the group of the specified directory only.

**Changing a group does not mean changing rights.** File `600` after `chgrp` remains `600`.

---

**11. `chown`: change owner and/or group**

Basic forms:

| Command | Action |
|---|---|
| `chown jane file` | Changes the owner user |
| `chown jane:users file` | Changes user and group |
| `chown :users file` | Changes group only |

**Changing the owner user is usually only possible with administrative rights.**

A regular user cannot simply transfer their file to another user.

**Owner user only:**

```console
# chown jane /tmp/filetest1
# ls -l /tmp/filetest1
-rw-rw-r-- 1 jane sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 /tmp/filetest1
```

Group `sysadmin` preserved.

**User and group:**

```console
# chown jane:users /tmp/filetest2
# ls -l /tmp/filetest2
-rw-rw-r-- 1 jane users 0 Nov 11 10:05 /tmp/filetest2
```

**Group only:**

```console
jane@localhost:~$ chown :users /tmp/filetest1
jane@localhost:~$ ls -l /tmp/filetest1
-rw-rw-r-- 1 jane users 0 Nov 11 10:00 /tmp/filetest1
```

In the latter case, restrictions similar to `chgrp`: file ownership and available group.

**Laboratory correction:** phrase «`chown` can only execute root» is too wide. Changing a user requires privileges, but the group-only modification form can be accessed by the owner.

The source also shows historical forms with a dot:

```text
chown jane.users file
chown .users file
```

For unambiguous modern notation, use a colon:

```text
jane:users
:users
```

Colon forms are described in [documentation `chown`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/chown.1.html).

---

**12. What do they mean? `r`, `w`, `x` for file**

| Right | Title | Action for a regular file |
|---|---|---|
| `r` | Read | Read content |
| `w` | Write | Change content |
| `x` | Execute | Run as program |

Example:

```text
rw- → can be read and modified, no direct execution rights
r-x → can be read and executed, no write permission
--- → these rights are not granted
```

**Source correction:** write to file **does not necessarily require reading**.

For example, a file might have:

```text
-w-
```

and allow writing without reading. Some editors require additional permissions due to the way they save, but this is not a general file system rule.

**Right `w` on a file does not equal the right to delete the file.**

---

**13. What do they mean? `r`, `w`, `x` for directory**

For the directory the values are different:

| Right | What allows |
|---|---|
| `r` | Get a list of names inside a directory |
| `w` | Modify directory entries: create, delete, rename |
| `x` | Walk through a directory and refer to known names inside |

**`x` on the directory - search/traverse permission.**

This allows a directory to be used as part of the path:

```text
/data/report.txt
```

**Typical combinations:**

| Directory permissions | Features |
|---|---|
| `r--` | You can find out the names, but you cannot normally access objects by these names |
| `--x` | You can refer to a known name if the target object’s rights allow |
| `r-x` | List of names and access to objects |
| `-wx` | You can edit records by known names without getting the full list |
| `rwx` | List, pass and change entries |

To create and delete records, you usually need **`w` and `x` together**.

---

**14. Which trio of rights applies**

Procedure for checking ordinary rights:

```text
1. Are you the owner?
   Yes → user applies.

2. Otherwise, are you part of the file group?
   Yes → group applies.

3. Otherwise → others is applied.
```

**The rights of different triplets do not add up.**

Example:

```text
----rw-rwx 1 bob bob ... abc.txt
```

Parsing:

```text
Type: -
Owner:   ---
Group:   rw-
Others:  rwx
```

Bob — owner, so for him select:

```text
---
```

You can’t say: «Bob is part of the bob group, so let’s take `rw-`» or «for the rest `rwx`, means he has it too».

**If the selected triple denies the action, there is no transition to a more generous triple.** [Description of rights check](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/path_resolution.7.html)

In this case, the owner can usually change the mode through `chmod`, even if it doesn’t have one right now `r` or `w` to the content.

---

**15. Check the entire path, not just the file**

To read:

```text
/data/project/report.txt
```

is usually required:

```text
x to /
x to /data
x on /data/project
r to report.txt
```

**Owning a file does not replace the need to traverse directories.**

Table of common requirements:

| Action | Rights |
|---|---|
| Read file | `x` on path directories and `r` on file |
| Write to existing file | `x` on path directories and `w` on file |
| Execute file directly | `x` on directory paths and file execution permissions |
| Go to directory via `cd` | `x` on it and path directories |
| Get list of names | `r` on the directory and access it |
| Get file details via `ls -l` | Usually `r` and `x` on the directory being viewed |
| Create file | `w+x` on the parent directory |
| Delete file name | Usually `w+x` on the parent directory |

`ls -l` without access to objects may show names with errors or unknown attributes instead of a complete list.

---

**16. Removal: the most important exam trap**

Remove file name - change **parent directory**.

Therefore the file:

```text
-r-------- 1 alice users ... report.txt
```

can be deleted by another user if he has the necessary rights to the parent directory and there are no additional restrictions.

And vice versa:

```text
-rw-rw-rw-
```

does not guarantee the ability to delete if there is no `w+x`.

**Example command `rm` — delete file.**

```console
$ rm /data/report.txt
$
```

On success there is usually no output.

If directory rights are not enough:

```text
rm: cannot remove '/data/report.txt': Permission denied
```

**Exception already visible in the lab: sticky bit.**

```text
drwxrwxrwt ... /tmp
```

Letter `t` means an additional deletion restriction: for an ordinary user it is not enough only `w+x`; usually it must own the file or the directory itself. A privileged process has separate capabilities. [Description sticky bit](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/chmod.1.html#RESTRICTED_DELETION_FLAG_OR_STICKY_BIT)

Nested `pub-dir` with mode `777` without sticky bit **does not automatically receive this protection from `/tmp`**.

---

**17. All six situations from the chapter**

We assume a regular user bob, who is not a member of the group root. Additional membership payroll is considered separately.

**Situation 1: the file belongs to bob, but there is no path through the directory**

```text
drwxr-xr-x root root /
drwxr-xr-- root root /data
-rwxr-xr-- bob  bob  /data/abc.txt
```

For bob on `/data` rights others apply:

```text
r--
```

No `x`, so it can’t access `abc.txt` along this path.

**Answer: no access to file contents**, despite `rwx` file owner.

---

**Situation 2: is it possible to get a list of names `/data`?**

Same rights:

```text
drwxr-xr-- root root /data
```

others has `r`.

**Answer: names can be obtained**, including hidden when used `ls -a`.

But without `x` it is impossible to obtain complete information about files and access them by name.

---

**Situation 3: everyone has `w`, but not everyone has it `x`**

```text
drwxr-xr-x root root /
drwxrw-rw- root root /data
-rwxr-xr-- bob  bob  /data/abc.txt
```

For group and others:

```text
rw-
```

Write permission is present, but directory search permission is missing.

**Chapter’s answer: root can delete.** Ordinary users do not have enough `x` on `/data`.

Ownership `abc.txt` does not correct missing passage.

---

**Situation 4: there is no list of names, but the path is known**

```text
drwxr-xr-x root root /
dr-xr-x--x root root /data
-rwxr-xr-- bob  bob  /data/abc.txt
```

bob has `/data`:

```text
--x
```

On the file as the owner:

```text
rwx
```

**Command `more /data/abc.txt` — view content.**

```console
$ more /data/abc.txt
Example text
```

**Reply: Read allowed.** The name is known, access is available, the file has the right to read. `r` on the directory is not required for this.

---

**Situation 5: supplementary groups unknown**

```text
drwxr-xr-x root root    /
dr-xr-x--- sue  payroll /data
-rwxr-xr-- bob  bob     /data/abc.txt
```

**Answer: not enough information.**

- bob is included in payroll → on `/data` receives `r-x`, file can be read;
- is not included → receives `---`, no access.

Need to check:

```console
$ id bob
uid=1002(bob) gid=1002(bob) groups=1002(bob),1007(payroll)
```

Here bob is included in payroll.

---

**Situation 6: the rights of others are greater than the rights of the owner**

```text
drwxr-xr-x root root /
dr-xr-x--- bob  bob  /data
----rw-rwx bob  bob  /data/abc.txt
```

There is a path to the file, but bob is its owner and receives:

```text
---
```

**Answer: it is impossible to read without changing the rights.** Group and others are not used as a fallback.

---

**18. `chmod`: who can change permissions**

**`chmod` — change mode**, change the access mode.

General syntax:

```text
chmod file mode
```

Permissions can usually be changed by:

- object owner;
- user with appropriate administrative rights.

**Having the right to write does not automatically give the right to change the mode.**

A user who is allowed to edit someone else’s file via `w`, does not become its owner.

`chmod` applies to both files and directories.

---

**19. Symbolic method `chmod`**

Formula:

```text
to whom + how + what _ rights
```

**To:**

| Symbol | Category |
|---|---|
| `u` | User owner — owner |
| `g` | Group — group |
| `o` | Others — others |
| `a` | All — all three categories |

**How to:**

| Operator | Action |
|---|---|
| `+` | Add specified rights |
| `-` | Remove the specified rights |
| `=` | Set the exact rights of the selected category |

**Which ones:**

```text
r → read
w → entry
x → execution / pass
```

**`u` — is the owner of the file, and not necessarily the person issuing the command.**

**`o` — others, and not owner.**

---

**20. Character commands with results**

For each line below, the original permissions are listed separately.

| Command | Description | Was → became |
|---|---|---|
| `chmod g+w file` | Add entry to group | `644 → 664` |
| `chmod a+x file` | Add execution to everyone | `644 → 755` |
| `chmod g-w file` | Remove group write permission | `664 → 644` |
| `chmod go+r file` | Add reading to group and others | `600 → 644` |
| `chmod o=rwx file` | Set others exactly `rwx` | `640 → 647` |
| `chmod a=rw file` | Everyone is sure to read and write | `754 → 666` |
| `chmod g-rw,o-r file` | Remove `rw` group and `r` to the rest | `664 → 600` |
| `chmod u+x file` | Add execution to owner | `664 → 764` |

**In the laboratory example `chmod o=rwx` filename missing.** The complete command must contain an object.

**Sequence from the chapter:**

```console
$ ls -l abc.txt
-rw-r--r-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 abc.txt

$ chmod g+w abc.txt
$ ls -l abc.txt
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 abc.txt
```

Next:

```console
$ chmod ug+x,o-r abc.txt
$ ls -l abc.txt
-rwxrwx--- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 abc.txt
```

Next:

```console
$ chmod u=rx abc.txt
$ ls -l abc.txt
-r-xrwx--- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 abc.txt
```

**`=` removes unspecified normal rights from the selected category only.**

In the last command:

- owner becomes `r-x`;
- group remains `rwx`;
- others remains `---`.

---

**21. Numeric method: `r=4`, `w=2`, `x=1`**

Each triple is written as a sum:

```text
r = 4
w = 2
x = 1
```

| Number | Rights | Calculation |
|---:|---|---|
| 0 | `---` | 0 |
| 1 | `--x` | 1 |
| 2 | `-w-` | 2 |
| 3 | `-wx` | 2 + 1 |
| 4 | `r--` | 4 |
| 5 | `r-x` | 4 + 1 |
| 6 | `rw-` | 4 + 2 |
| 7 | `rwx` | 4 + 2 + 1 |

Three digits:

```text
owner group others
```

Example:

```text
754
││└─ others: r--
│└── group:  r-x
└─── owner:  rwx
```

**Command `chmod 754 abc.txt` — set the exact customary rights.**

```console
$ chmod 754 abc.txt
$ ls -l abc.txt
-rwxr-xr-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 abc.txt
```

The numeric method is useful when you need to set all nine regular bits at once.

---

**22. Frequent modes to recognize**

| Mode | Character entry | Meaning |
|---:|---|---|
| `600` | `rw-------` | Only owner reads and writes |
| `640` | `rw-r-----` | Owner reads/writes, group reads |
| `644` | `rw-r--r--` | The owner writes, everyone reads |
| `664` | `rw-rw-r--` | Owner and group write, others read |
| `666` | `rw-rw-rw-` | Everyone reads and writes |
| `700` | `rwx------` | Full owner access |
| `750` | `rwxr-x---` | Owner in full, group reads/passes |
| `755` | `rwxr-xr-x` | Owner in full, others read/execute |
| `764` | `rwxrw-r--` | Intermediate script mode in laboratory |
| `770` | `rwxrwx---` | Owner and group in full |
| `775` | `rwxrwxr-x` | Owner and group in full, others read/execute |
| `777` | `rwxrwxrwx` | All normal rights to everyone |

For directory `x` means pass, so the same numbers have different practical implications for a file and a directory.

**`777` — is not a universal fix for access problems.** It provides an entry for all categories.

---

**23. Script execution: `./test.sh`**

A file with the command is created in the laboratory `date`.

**Command `echo "date" > test.sh` — write a line to a file.**

```console
$ echo "date" > test.sh
$ ls -l test.sh
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 5 Nov 11 12:00 test.sh
```

Size 5 bytes:

```text
date + line feed
```

`>` creates a file or overwrites existing content.

**Direct start attempt:**

```console
$ ./test.sh
bash: ./test.sh: Permission denied
```

No `x` for the owner.

**Adding execution to the owner:**

```console
$ chmod u+x test.sh
$ ls -l test.sh
-rwxrw-r-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 5 Nov 11 12:00 test.sh
```

Now:

```console
$ ./test.sh
Wed Nov 11 12:30:00 +05 2026
```

`./` specifies a file in the current directory.

**Command `chmod 775 test.sh` — set the mode from the next lab step.**

```console
$ chmod 775 test.sh
$ ls -l test.sh
-rwxrwxr-x 1 sysadmin sysadmin 5 Nov 11 12:00 test.sh
```

---

**24. Important clarification: the script can be read by an interpreter**

Source approval «commands inside a file can only be executed if there is `x`» too broad.

If the file is readable, it can be passed to the shell:

```console
$ bash test.sh
Wed Nov 11 12:30:00 +05 2026
```

For this method myself `test.sh` is not required to have `x`: program is being executed `bash`, which reads the text.

Difference:

```text
./test.sh    → direct file launch, x required
bash test.sh → interpreter reads file
```

A regular shell-script also requires the ability to read its text.

The laboratory script does not contain `#!`. Bash can process such text after startup failure in a recognized executable format; so the example works in the specified shell. [Documentation Bash](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/bash.1.html)

Right `x` does not by itself make arbitrary data a valid program; Additional restrictions may apply.

---

**25. `stat`: rights, UID/GID and timestamps**

**Command `stat test.sh` — detailed information about the file.**

```console
$ stat test.sh
  File: test.sh
  Size: 5          Blocks: 8          IO Block: 4096 regular file
Device: 802h/2050d  Inode: 3943515     Links: 1
Access: (0764/-rwxrw-r--)  Uid: (1001/sysadmin)  Gid: (1001/sysadmin)
Access: 2026-11-11 12:30:00.000000000 +0500
Modify: 2026-11-11 12:00:00.000000000 +0500
Change: 2026-11-11 12:01:00.000000000 +0500
 Birth: -
```

**It is especially important for the exam:**

```text
Access: (0764/-rwxrw-r--)
```

One mode is shown in two ways:

```text
764         → numeric
rwxrw-r--   → character
```

Fields:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Size` | Size |
| `Inode` | Number inode |
| `Links` | Number of hard links |
| `Uid` | UID and owner name |
| `Gid` | GID and group name |
| `Access` with date | Access time |
| `Modify` | Content change time |
| `Change` | State/metadata change time inode |
| `Birth` | Creation time, if available |

**`Change` — is not the creation date.**

Don’t confuse the first line `Access` with access mode and the next line `Access` with a timestamp.

---

**26. `umask`: rights when creating**

**`umask` specifies which normal permission bits will be removed when new objects are created.**

For typical commands:

```text
New regular file: requesting 666
New directory: requesting 777
```

That is:

```text
File: rw-rw-rw-
directory: rwxrwxrwx
```

**Command `umask` without argument - show the current mask.**

```console
$ umask
0002
```

**Command `umask 027` — set the mask for the current shell.**

```console
$ umask 027
$
```

If successful, there is no separate output.

**The mask contains prohibited bits, not ready-made rights.**

```text
chmod 640 file → set permissions 640
umask 027      → remove the specified bits from the rights of new objects
```

---

**27. Why `umask` — not normal subtraction**

The source material uses a simplified «maximum minus umask».

Exact operation:

```text
total = requested _ rights AND NOT umask
```

Simpler:

> Each set umask bit removes the corresponding right.

Example `027`:

| Category | Mask | What’s being removed |
|---|---|---|
| Owner | `0` | Nothing |
| Group | `2` | Write |
| Others | `7` | That’s it |

For a regular file:

```text
Requested: rw- rw- rw-
Removed: --- -w- rwx
Result: rw- r-- ---
           6   4   0
```

For the directory:

```text
Requested: rwx rwx rwx
Removed: --- -w- rwx
Result: rwx r-x ---
           7   5   0
```

**Counterexample to normal subtraction:**

```text
File request: 666
umask:       111
Result: 666
```

The mask only removes `x`, which is not in the request anyway. The result is not `555`.

This behavior and mask inheritance by processes are described in [documentation `umask`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/umask.2.html).

---

**28. Table `umask`, worth learning**

For normal creation of a request file `666` and the directory with the request `777`, without influence default ACL:

| Umask | New file | Symbolic | New directory | Symbolic |
|---|---:|---|---:|---|
| `000` | `666` | `rw-rw-rw-` | `777` | `rwxrwxrwx` |
| `002` | `664` | `rw-rw-r--` | `775` | `rwxrwxr-x` |
| `022` | `644` | `rw-r--r--` | `755` | `rwxr-xr-x` |
| `027` | `640` | `rw-r-----` | `750` | `rwxr-x---` |
| `077` | `600` | `rw-------` | `700` | `rwx------` |
| `777` | `000` | `---------` | `000` | `---------` |

**Example from the chapter:**

```console
$ umask 027
$ touch sample
$ ls -l sample
-rw-r----- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 sample
```

For the directory:

```console
$ mkdir test-dir
$ ls -ld test-dir
drwxr-x--- 2 sysadmin sysadmin 4096 Nov 11 10:00 test-dir
```

It is assumed here that `sample` and `test-dir` did not exist yet.

**`umask` does not change the rights of existing objects.** For example, `touch` of the old file does not recalculate its mode using the new mask.

---

**29. Clarifications about initial rights and retention `umask`**

**Not all programs are required to create files with the request `666`.**

This is a typical request for `touch` and output redirection, but the program may request a more restrictive mode or create an executable file.

Therefore, the source statement «the initial permissions of any file cannot exceed 666» is incorrect as a general rule.

**The mask refers to the process:**

- change via builtin command shell affects the current shell;
- child processes inherit it;
- shell startup settings may reset the mask.

It cannot be assumed that any new child shell will necessarily automatically return «original» mask.

For reuse, the value is placed in a suitable startup file, for example:

```bash
umask 027
```

In Bash such a file can be `.bashrc`, but this **is not the only possible place**: selection depends on shell type, login mode, and system settings.

---

**30. First part of the lab: files and rights**

Initial mask assumed `002`, as in the learning environment output.

**Go to `/tmp`:**

```console
$ cd /tmp
$
```

`cd` usually prints nothing if successful.

**Creating directories:**

```console
$ mkdir priv-dir pub-dir
$
```

**Creating files:**

```console
$ touch priv-dir/priv-file
$ touch pub-dir/pub-file
$
```

Check:

```console
$ ls -l priv-dir
total 0
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 priv-file

$ ls -l pub-dir
total 0
-rw-rw-r-- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 pub-file
```

**Changes from the lab:**

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `chmod o-rx priv-dir` | Directory `775 → 770` |
| `chmod o+w pub-dir` | Directory `775 → 777` |
| `chmod g-rw,o-r priv-dir/priv-file` | File `664 → 600` |
| `chmod a=rw pub-dir/pub-file` | File `664 → 666` |
| `chmod u+x test.sh` | Script `664 → 764` |
| `chmod 775 test.sh` | Script `764 → 775` |

Checking directories:

```console
$ ls -ld priv-dir pub-dir
drwxrwx--- 2 sysadmin sysadmin 4096 Nov 11 10:00 priv-dir
drwxrwxrwx 2 sysadmin sysadmin 4096 Nov 11 10:00 pub-dir
```

Checking files:

```console
$ ls -l priv-dir/priv-file pub-dir/pub-file
-rw------- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 priv-dir/priv-file
-rw-rw-rw- 1 sysadmin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 pub-dir/pub-file
```

**`priv-dir` is closed from others, but the group still has `rwx`.** Name `priv-dir` in itself does not mean exclusive access to the owner.

---

**31. Second part of the laboratory: possession**

**Go to root:**

```console
$ su -
Password:
root@localhost:~#
```

Study Environment Password - `netlab123`.

After `su -` is moving to the home directory root, so again we need:

```console
# cd /tmp
#
```

**Change owner and group of directory only `pub-dir`:**

```console
# chown root:root pub-dir
# ls -ld pub-dir
drwxrwxrwx 2 root root 4096 Nov 11 10:00 pub-dir
```

**Content has not changed automatically**, because the recursive operation was not performed.

**Change file owner user to bin:**

```console
# chown bin pub-dir/pub-file
# ls -l pub-dir/pub-file
-rw-rw-rw- 1 bin sysadmin 0 Nov 11 10:00 pub-dir/pub-file
```

Group `sysadmin` preserved.

**Change private tree group recursively:**

```console
# chgrp -R users priv-dir
# ls -ld priv-dir
drwxrwx--- 2 sysadmin users 4096 Nov 11 10:00 priv-dir

# ls -l priv-dir/priv-file
-rw------- 1 sysadmin users 0 Nov 11 10:00 priv-dir/priv-file
```

**There is an error in the last output from the original lab.** After `chgrp -R` the directory does not turn into a regular file, and its rights do not become `600`. The group is changing, not the type or normal rights.

---

**32. Resulting laboratory objects**

After all steps:

| Object | Owner | Group | Rights |
|---|---|---|---|
| `priv-dir` | sysadmin | users | `770`, `rwxrwx---` |
| `priv-dir/priv-file` | sysadmin | users | `600`, `rw-------` |
| `pub-dir` | root | root | `777`, `rwxrwxrwx` |
| `pub-dir/pub-file` | bin | sysadmin | `666`, `rw-rw-rw-` |
| `test.sh` | sysadmin | sysadmin | `775`, `rwxrwxr-x` |

**Please note:** group users can pass in `priv-dir`, but doesn’t get read `priv-file`, because the file has group- permissions `---`.

---

**33. Common mistakes on the exam**

| Incorrect statement | Correct |
|---|---|
| The owner always has all rights | owner-troika is used for it |
| Rights owner, group and others add up | One suitable category is selected |
| If owner is prohibited, you can take others | No |
| `r` directory allows you to open any file | Passage and permissions of the file itself are required |
| `x` directory is needed only for `cd` | It is needed to refer to names along the path |
| To register, you must `r` | Write can be allowed without reading |
| `w` of a file allows you to delete it | Removal depends on the directory |
| `rwx` file is sufficient without directory rights | Need passage along the way |
| Hidden file is read-protected | The dot hides the name from the regular list |
| `chgrp` changes permissions | Changes group |
| `chown jane file` also changes the group | Without the specified group, it is saved |
| `newgrp` constantly overwrites passwd | Changes the group of the new shell |
| `chmod o=rw` adds read/write, saving x | `=` will also remove x from others |
| `umask 027` sets the rights 027 | The mask removes bits from the requested rights |
| Umask — normal subtraction | This is a bit operation |
| New umask modifies old files | No |
| Any new file must have a maximum of 666 | This is a typical request from some programs |
| A script without x cannot be read through Bash | `bash script` requires reading, not x of the text itself |
| Recursive group change changes directory type | No |

---

**34. Self-check Questions — with Answers**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What are the two owners of the file? | User and group |
| What is stored as the owners’ identity? | UID and GID |
| How can I see the owners? | `ls -l` or `stat` |
| How to view the directory itself? | `ls -ld directory` |
| How do I enable hidden names? | `ls -a` |
| What does the first one mean? `-` in `-rw-r--r--`? | Regular file |
| What does it mean? `d`? | Directory |
| What does it mean? `l`? | Symbolic link |
| What does it mean? `b`? | Block device |
| What does it mean? `c`? | Character device |
| What does it mean? `p`? | FIFO |
| What does it mean? `s`? | Socket |
| What does it mean? `u` to chmod? | Owner |
| What does it mean? `g`? | Group |
| What does it mean? `o`? | Others |
| What does it mean? `a`? | All three categories |
| What does it do? `+`? | Adds the specified rights |
| What does it do? `-`? | Removes the specified rights |
| What does it do? `=`? | Sets the exact category permissions |
| Number to read? | 4 |
| For the record? | 2 |
| For execution? | 1 |
| What does 7 mean? | `rwx` |
| What does 6 mean? | `rw-` |
| What does 5 mean? | `r-x` |
| What does 3 mean? | `-wx` |
| How to record `rw-r-----`? | 640 |
| How to record `rwxr-xr-x`? | 755 |
| How to record `rwxrw-r--`? | 764 |
| How to record `rwxrwx---`? | 770 |
| How to add x to the owner? | `chmod u+x file` |
| How do you remove write permission from the group? | `chmod g-w file` |
| How to give everyone exactly rw? | `chmod a=rw file` |
| Who can usually perform chmod? | Owner and Super User |
| Does writing to a file give you the right to change its mode? | No |
| What does r mean in the catalogue? | Get names |
| What does x mean in the catalogue? | Walking and accessing names |
| What does w mean in the catalogue? | Changing entries |
| What normal rights are needed to delete a name? | `w+x` on the parent directory |
| Is w needed on the file itself to be deleted? | Usually no |
| Why can’t you freely delete other people’s files in /tmp? | Sticky bit |
| What three is used for the owner? | Owner |
| Is it counted as group/others instead of owner? | No |
| Is it possible to read a known file in a directory without r? | Yes, if there is x and file permissions |
| Can you read your file without x on the parent directory? | Not this way |
| How can I temporarily change the current group? | `newgrp group` |
| How to return after newgrp? | `exit` |
| How do I change the group of a file? | `chgrp group file` |
| How do I change the tree group? | `chgrp -R group directory` |
| How do I change the owner user? | `chown user file` |

| How can I view numeric and symbolic permissions at the same time? | `stat file` |

| With umask 022 a regular new file? | 644 |
| With umask 022 new directory? | 755 |
| When umask 027 file? | 640 |
| With umask 027 directory? | 750 |
| When umask 077 file? | 600 |
| With umask 077 directory? | 700 |

| Does chmod change owners? | No |
| Does chgrp change normal permissions? | No |

title: Special Directories and Files
summary: SUID, SGID, sticky bit, inode and links
markdown:
Read completely **chapter 18 and laboratory 18**. Below is a summary of all their contents: special rights, temporary directories, inode, hard and symbolic links, commands with examples and questions for self-test.

**All output examples are educational.** inode numbers, program sizes, dates and system settings may vary. I did not run the commands from the documents.

There are several inaccuracies in the source material - they are corrected and explained below.

---

**1. What you need to know for the exam**

The topic is indicated in the chapter **5.4 — Special Directories and Files**, weight - **1**.

Basic knowledge:

- destination `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`;
- special bits `setuid`, `setgid`, `sticky bit`;
- designations `s`, `S`, `t`, `T`;
- four-digit numeric rights record;
- destination inode;
- creating hard and symbolic links;
- differences between them;
- consequences of deleting a filename or link target.

Main commands:

```text
chmod
ls -l
ls -ld
ls -i
ls -li
ln
ln -s
rm
find
```

---

**2. Three special bits**

Regular rights:

```text
r → read
w → entry
x → execute / walk through directory
```

Additionally there are:

| Bit | Numeric value | Main purpose |
|---|---:|---|
| **setuid — SUID** | `4000` | Program execution with effective owner UID |
| **setgid — SGID** | `2000` | Running with effective group GID or inheriting a group in a directory |
| **sticky bit** | `1000` | Limit deleting and renaming entries in the shared directory |

**They do not replace normal permissions.**

For example, setgid of a directory does not grant the user the right to enter it if normal rights do not give `x`.

---

**3. Four digits in numeric notation**

Example:

```text
2775
│││└─ others: r-x
││└── group:  rwx
│└─── owner:  rwx
└──── special bits: setgid
```

The last three digits work as in chapter 17:

```text
r = 4
w = 2
x = 1
```

The first digit consists of:

```text
setuid = 4
setgid = 2
sticky = 1
```

| First digit | Special bits set |
|---:|---|
| `0` | No |
| `1` | Sticky |
| `2` | Setgid |
| `3` | Setgid + sticky |
| `4` | Setuid |
| `5` | Setuid + sticky |
| `6` | Setuid + setgid |
| `7` | All three |

The practical meaning depends on the type of object. For example, sticky bit is discussed in this topic **on directories**.

**Examples of modes:**

| Mode | Typical display example |
|---:|---|
| `4755` | `-rwsr-xr-x` |
| `4775` | `-rwsrwxr-x` |
| `2755` | `-rwxr-sr-x` |
| `2775` for directory | `drwxrwsr-x` |
| `1777` for directory | `drwxrwxrwt` |
| `1770` for directory | `drwxrwx--T` |
| `3770` for directory | `drwxrws--T` |

---

**4. Where special bits are displayed**

They use the positions of the regular `x`.

```text
- rwx rwx rwx
    │   │   │
    │   │   └─ sticky: t / T
    │   └───── setgid: s / S
    └───────── setuid: s / S
```

| Symbol | What does it mean? |
|---|---|
| `s` at owner- position | Setuid and owner `x` installed |
| `S` at owner- position | Setuid installed, owner `x` missing |
| `s` at group- position | Setgid and group `x` installed |
| `S` at group- position | Setgid installed, group `x` missing |
| `t` at others- position | Sticky and others `x` installed |
| `T` at others- position | Sticky installed, others `x` missing |

**Small letter → corresponding `x` is.**

**Capital letter → corresponding `x` no.**

A capital letter does not mean that the special bit is missing.

---

**5. Setuid: what happens when the program starts**

During normal startup, the program works with the identifiers of the calling process.

When running the executable binary from setuid:

```text
effective UID → UID program owner
```

For example:

```text
User sysadmin starts the program.
The program belongs to root.
setuid is installed on the program.
→ The program receives an effective UID root.
```

**This does not turn the entire user shell into root.** The change applies to the program being executed.

Also, setuid does not have to mean root: the owner of the program can be another user.

The exact rule concerns **effective UID**; the real UID of the calling user does not necessarily change. [Program launch documentation](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html)

---

**6. Why can a regular user change his password?**

A normal user cannot directly read `/etc/shadow`.

**Command `more /etc/shadow` — try to view the file.**

```console
$ more /etc/shadow
/etc/shadow: Permission denied
```

**Command `ls -l /etc/shadow` — see owner and rights.**

```console
$ ls -l /etc/shadow
-rw-r----- 1 root shadow 968 Nov 11 09:00 /etc/shadow
```

But the user can do:

**11. Subdirectories also inherit setgid**

Inside the SGID- directory, the new subdirectory usually receives:

1. parent directory group;
2. own installed setgid.

**15. Sticky bit: deletion restriction**

From chapter 17:

```text
w+x on a directory → ability to change directory entries
```

Without sticky bit, a user with such rights can delete other people’s file names, even if the files themselves do not belong to him.

**Sticky bit adds restrictions on deleting and renaming.**

In a normal case, this operation can be performed by:

- file owner;
- owner of the containing directory;
- privileged process.

**Source correction:** takes into account not only the owner of the file and root, but also **directory owner**. [Description sticky bit](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/chmod.1.html#RESTRICTED_DELETION_FLAG_OR_STICKY_BIT)

The required normal access rights are still required.

**Sticky bit does not prohibit reading or changing the contents of someone else’s file**, if its own rights permit it. It restricts operations on directory names.

**20. Why do we need links?**

Let’s assume the file is deep:

```text
/usr/share/doc/package/data/reports/important.txt
```

You want to refer to it by its short name in your home directory.

A copy is not always suitable: it will become a separate object and may become obsolete.

A link provides another way to access data or a path.

There are two types:

| View | Another name | Base |
|---|---|---|
| Hard link | Hard link | Another name of the same inode |
| Symbolic link | Soft link, symlink | Single object with path to target |

**21. Inode and directory entry**

**Inode** — file system structure containing information about the object:

- type;
- rights;
- UID and GID;
- size;
- timestamps;
- number of hard links;
- data access information.

**Name is in directory entry**, which links it to inode.

Simplified:

```text
directory name → inode → data
```

Example:

```text
source → inode 6689431 → "data"
```

**Inode number is unique within the file system**, and not necessarily throughout the entire computer.

Two different file systems may have the same object number inode. [Documentation inode](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/inode.7.html)

**Clarification of source terminology:** separate file has inode; inode table is a table of such structures, and not the name of the metadata of one file.

**26. Hard Link Limitations**

**First: one file system.**

You cannot do hard link between different file systems.

Example if `/boot` is indeed mounted separately and the file exists:

```console
$ ln /boot/vmlinuz-demo Linux.Kernel
ln: failed to create hard link 'Linux.Kernel': Invalid cross-device link
```

**The path itself `/boot` does not guarantee an error:** reason is a file system boundary, not a directory name.

**Second: regular hard links directories are not created.**

```console
$ ln /bin binary
ln: /bin: hard link not allowed for directory
```

For the purposes of this course, remember:

```text
hard link → existing file, on the same file system
```

Also, the creation of links may be limited by rights and system security settings.

**30. Relative and absolute target symlink**

**Absolute target:**

```console
$ ln -s /home/sysadmin/source /tmp/soft-absolute
$ ls -l /tmp/soft-absolute
lrwxrwxrwx 1 sysadmin sysadmin 21 Nov 11 10:20 /tmp/soft-absolute -> /home/sysadmin/source
```

The path starts from `/`.

**Relative target:**

```console
$ ln -s source softlink
$ ls -l softlink
lrwxrwxrwx 1 sysadmin sysadmin 6 Nov 11 10:20 softlink -> source
```

**The relative target is resolved from the directory of the link itself**, and not from the user’s current directory at the time of subsequent reading.

For example:

```text
/home/sysadmin/softlink -> source
```

indicates:

```text
/home/sysadmin/source
```

But:

```text
/tmp/softlink -> source
```

will search for:

```text
/tmp/source
```

This rule is important when moving links. [Documentation `ln`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/ln.1.html)

**33. Symbolic link permissions**

Typically seen:

```text
lrwxrwxrwx
```

**This does not mean that everyone has full access to the target file.**

When reading normally via a link, the following are taken into account:

- path directory access;
- resolve link to target;
- rights of the target object.

For example:

```text
link -> /etc/shadow
```

does not allow a normal user to read shadow just because the link displays `777`.

In Linux, the normal rights symlink are not used as access rights to the target; in this case, the owner of the link itself may be important, for example, for its deletion in the sticky- directory. [Documentation symlink](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/symlink.7.html)

The link is not a way to bypass file permissions.

**34. Hard link and symbolic link: a complete comparison**

| Property | Hard link | Symbolic link |
|---|---|---|
| Creation | `ln target name` | `ln -s target name` |
| What does it represent? | Additional name of the same inode | Single object with path |
| Inode relative to target | Same | Own |
| Type in `ls -l` | Same as the file itself, usually `-` | `l` |
| Increases target link count | Yes | No |
| Requires an existing target | Yes | No |
| Possible between file systems | No | Yes |
| Available on the directory | Usually no | Yes |
| Visible `-> target` | No | Yes |
| Removing the original name | Other names work | Breaks if the target’s path disappears |
| Common rights and owners | Common to inode | Link and target have different objects |
| Delete link | Removes one file name | Removes symlink, the target remains |
| Copies target data | No | No |

**Basic formula:**

```text
Hard link → inode
Soft link → path
```

| Capital `S` means no special bit | There is a special bit, there is no corresponding x |
| Sticky prohibits reading other people’s files | Restricts deleting and renaming |

| `chmod 775` always removes the SGID directory | Security is possible in GNU; use explicit `g-s` |
| Hard link — copy | This is the name of the same inode |
| hard links has a mandatory main original | All names are equal |
| Inode is unique on the entire computer | Only within the file system |
| Removing the original name destroys hard link | No |
| Symlink has inode targets | She has her own inode |
| Symlink increases target count | No |
